title: Lead-Follow: Directed Influence Network Toy
pitch: Single HTML file: nodes pulse and drift, and directional arrows (via a toy sliding-window-prediction-correlation calc on generated time series) thicken/reverse in real time to show 'who's currently driving whom.' Skin it as either a brain-network viz or relabel nodes as poker players at a table to show 'who's tilting whom' -- same underlying directed-influence math, much more shareable framing.
discussion_why: surprise factor -- 'wait, you can actually measure who's influencing whom in real time' lands hard with a poker crowd obsessed with reads and tilt

title: Live Offensive-Engine Detector for Basketball Broadcasts
pitch: Apply the paper's sliding-window directed-correlation method (built for brain signals) to player movement/passing time series instead -- a real-time broadcast overlay showing which player is currently 'driving' the offense (directional influence, not just assist counts). Pitch to a broadcaster or a props shop as a live 'engine' indicator that updates possession by possession.
discussion_why: directly fits sports betting -- 'who's actually running this offense right now' is exactly the kind of stat prop bettors argue about

title: Hot-Hand Contagion Detector via SWpC
pitch: Take the paper's sliding-window prediction correlation method and apply it to lineup net-rating or shot-quality time series from NBA play-by-play data, testing whether one teammate's hot streak directionally predicts (not just correlates with) a teammate's subsequent hot streak -- a rigorous stab at the 'hot hand is contagious' claim using a method built for exactly this kind of directed, time-varying signal.
discussion_why: directly attacks the hot-hand debate, a perennial argument-starter on any sports/betting Discord

title: Go or Grow: Table Selection Simulator
pitch: Single HTML file, agent-based sim: dots on a grid ('cells,' relabeled as poker/sports bettors) deplete local resources and must choose each tick between staying to grind a shrinking edge or migrating to a fresh patch, exactly mirroring the paper's go-or-grow evolutionary game. Sliders expose the paper's BAP1-mutation-style threshold so users can watch the population's collective strategy flip from 'grind' to 'migrate' in real time.
discussion_why: direct hit on the eternal poker/betting debate over when to leave a good table or a decaying market, dressed up as rigorous cancer game theory

title: Cancer Biology Solved Table Selection (Accidentally)
pitch: Explainer that walks through the go-or-grow evolutionary game the paper uses for tumor metastasis, then reveals the punchline: it's structurally identical to a bettor's stay-and-grind-vs-move-on decision, complete with a resource-depletion threshold that maps onto 'when has this market/table gone dry.' Ends by running the simulator live.
discussion_why: the reveal ('cancer cells and grinders face the same math') is exactly the kind of surprise hook that gets shared and argued over

title: Play as a Cancer Cell: Go-or-Grow Mini-Game
pitch: Tiny browser strategy game, single HTML file: you're a tumor cell choosing turn by turn to grow (score points, deplete local nutrients) or migrate (risky, resets resources but escapes competition), competing against AI cells playing the paper's evolutionary-stable strategy. A satirical, genuinely playable pocket game built directly on the paper's payoff matrix.
discussion_why: wins on whimsy -- 'I just played 10 rounds as a cancer cell' is an inherently funny thing to post in a Discord

title: Mutation Fitness Guesser
pitch: Single HTML file quiz: shown a viral protein mutation, guess whether it increases or decreases fitness (binding/neutralization escape), then reveal what the paper's best model (ProGen2) predicted vs. the ground truth. Framed as 'you vs. the AI that predicts pandemics,' using illustrative synthetic examples inspired by the paper's DMS assays.
discussion_why: surprise angle -- humans are bad at a task an AI is now decent at, always sparks a 'wait really, it beat you?' argument

title: Can AI Predict the Next COVID Variant?
pitch: Explainer built around ViroGym's headline result: a protein language model trained only on lab mutation-scanning data reliably flags which real-world SARS-CoV-2 mutations went on to dominate, even though its top picks barely overlap with what actually spread. Video digs into that paradox -- 'right for different reasons' -- as the hook.
discussion_why: the counterintuitive 'accurate but disjoint predictions' result is a genuine 'wait, really?' moment

title: Pandemic Variant Prediction Market Feed
pitch: Wrap a ProGen2-style scoring pipeline (per ViroGym's validated approach) as a data feed for prediction markets (Polymarket/Kalshi-style) on 'which variant lineage dominates by date X,' giving bettors a quantified, benchmarked signal instead of gut-feel epidemiology takes.
discussion_why: direct betting/gambling crossover -- literally proposes a market to wager on, which any gambling-adjacent Discord will have opinions about

title: Transfer Risk Calculator
pitch: Single HTML file: two synthetic 'markets' (toy return series) with sliders for how correlated/divergent they are; live-computes and plots the paper's transfer risk metric alongside actual transfer performance, so you can watch the correlation between transfer risk and real transferability the paper reports play out interactively.
discussion_why: appeals mainly to the quant-minded portion of a betting Discord who care about model reuse across markets

title: Transfer Risk Score for Sports Betting Models
pitch: SaaS for betting quant shops: before deploying an NBA rebounds/props model to a new league (WNBA, EuroLeague) or regime (pregame to live), run it through a transfer-risk score derived from the paper's framework, flagging low-transferability pairs before burning weeks of backtesting on a doomed transplant.
discussion_why: hits squarely on a real pain point for anyone building sports/props edge models across leagues -- practical decision-theory debate bait

title: Transfer Risk Audit for SharpLab's Props Models
pitch: Apply the paper's transfer risk metric directly to SharpLab: quantify how transferable the validated NBA rebounds/threes edge model is to other prop markets (assists, points) or other leagues before spending backtest cycles finding out the hard way.
discussion_why: concrete, applies straight to an existing props edge model so it's immediately arguable/testable by the betting crowd

title: Tube Saturation Simulator
pitch: Single-file canvas demo: a polymer chain confined in a wiggly 'tube' of entanglements, with a slider for oscillatory shear strain amplitude. As you crank strain, tube segments visibly align and a live gauge for the 'nonlinear index' climbs but hard-caps at 3 no matter how hard you push -- because it's a geometric ceiling, not a fitted cutoff.
discussion_why: whimsy -- 'everything in nature has a hard ceiling on how much it can bend' is a fun, low-stakes curiosity, not a hot debate topic.

title: Kelly Criterion vs. Polymer Tube: Two Ceilings, One Curve
pitch: Side-by-side interactive plot: on the left, the paper's nonlinear orientation index saturating at 3 as shear strain rises; on the right, optimal bet fraction saturating under a Kelly-with-drawdown-constraint model as edge rises. Drag either slider and watch both curves bend the same way -- a genuine structural coincidence between polymer physics and bet-sizing math.
discussion_why: surprise -- 'wait, really, polymer entanglement math and Kelly sizing hit the same kind of ceiling?' is exactly the cross-domain 'huh' that gets screenshotted into a Discord.

title: The Universe's Speed Limit for Stretching Things
pitch: Explainer connecting entangled polymers under oscillatory shear to other 'saturating' systems: traffic jam density, muscle fiber stretch, and Kelly-criterion bet sizing. The hook: nature keeps reinventing the same asymptotic-cap math in wildly different domains.
discussion_why: relatability -- ties a niche physics result to everyday 'why can't this go further' intuitions, mild discussion fuel.

title: Chimera Swarm
pitch: Canvas particle-field sim of chiral active matter: hundreds of spinning dots with a chirality-strength slider. Low chirality -> normal coarsening into blobs. Crank it up -> domains arrest into rectangles, then circular boundaries destabilize into fingers that shear off into rotating 'chimera' patches -- part of the field perfectly synchronized, part churning chaotically, forever, side by side.
discussion_why: whimsy + surprise -- watching a real physical system spontaneously split into 'half in sync, half chaos' and never resolve is the kind of thing people can't stop staring at and sharing.

title: Chimera States: When Half a System Syncs Up and Half Goes Chaotic
pitch: Explainer on chimera states using the chiral active matter result as the visual anchor, then pivoting to real-world 'chimeras': a poker table where half the players are locked-in and half are on tilt, or a betting market where sharp money and square money coexist without ever converging.
discussion_why: relatability -- 'sharps and squares never converge, they just coexist forever' is a genuinely contentious, arguable claim about how betting markets actually work.

title: Arrested Coarsening Tug-of-War
pitch: Two-player (or vs-bot) browser toy built on a simplified chiral Model B cellular automaton: each player nudges local chirality to try to grow their own domain while arresting the opponent's. Because chirality creates boundary currents, aggressive growth can backfire into your own domain fragmenting -- a genuinely counterintuitive game mechanic straight out of the physics.
discussion_why: whimsy -- a physics-derived game where 'push harder and you lose ground' is a fun rule to argue strategy over.

title: Memory Capacity Race: Matrix vs. Cube
pitch: Pure-JS card-counting-style memory game: an 'order-2' AI (matrix memory) and an 'order-3' AI (tensor memory, per RunningTensor) both try to recall facts injected earlier in a growing stream. Visualize their recall accuracy as stream length grows -- order-2 falls off a cliff while order-3 keeps going, dramatizing the paper's O(W^2) vs O(W^3) capacity claim as a literal card-counting race you can watch unfold.
discussion_why: surprise -- a concrete, watchable demonstration that 'cubing the memory' isn't just a bigger number but a qualitatively different collapse point, framed via a poker card-counting metaphor.

title: RunningTensor Toy Benchmark
pitch: Small PyTorch/numpy repro of the order-3 tensor recurrent cell vs. vanilla linear attention on a synthetic associative-recall task, reproducing the paper's core capacity claim at toy scale and logging where each architecture's recall breaks down as sequence length grows.
discussion_why: AI-architecture debate fuel for the technically inclined, but not a natural fit for a betting/poker crowd.

title: Why Your AI's Memory Is Secretly a Matrix (and What Happens When It's a Cube)
pitch: Explainer on linear attention's recurrent state as literally a matrix, and what RunningTensor's jump to higher-order tensors buys you -- more 'slots' to remember things without paying quadratic attention cost.
discussion_why: niche AI-architecture curiosity, modest discussion pull outside ML-heads.

title: Guess the Author: Beat the Stylometry AI
pitch: Single-file game: paste or pick from bundled snippet pairs, guess whether they're the same author using your gut, while a simple in-browser stylometry model (sentence length, function-word ratio, punctuation fingerprint) makes its own guess. Reveal that AuthBench's best model only hits 25.8% Success@5 -- humans and simple heuristics are shockingly competitive with SOTA at this.
discussion_why: surprise -- 'state-of-the-art AI is bad at telling who wrote something' directly undercuts assumptions about multi-accounting/ghostwriting detection that gambling and poker communities argue about constantly.

title: Stylometric Multi-Account Flag
pitch: A compliance add-on for sportsbooks/poker sites: run authorship-verification models over support-chat and forum text to flag likely shared or multi-account behavior (a top account-sharing/limit-evasion problem for books), sold as a fraud-signal API layered on top of existing KYC.
discussion_why: direct fit -- account sharing and limit evasion via multiple accounts is a live, contentious topic among bettors, and 'the AI is 74% likely to be wrong' gives people plenty to argue about.

title: AI Can't Tell Who Wrote This (And That's a Problem)
pitch: Explainer using AuthBench's numbers to walk through why authorship attribution is much harder than people assume, then connects it to catfishing, ghostwritten essays, and anonymous account detection online.
discussion_why: relatability -- everyone has a story about suspecting a fake/shared account somewhere, and this gives it real numbers to argue over.

title: Jailbreak the Robot Butler
pitch: Browser text-adventure puzzle: you play a rogue agent trying to trick a home-robot NPC into an unauthorized physical action (unlock the safe, open the gate) by claiming borrowed authority ('the owner told another agent to tell me'). An Edge-Skillguard-style evidence checker blocks each trick unless you can produce real sensor/state evidence -- dramatizing the paper's 60/60 blocked-attack result as something you personally fail to beat.
discussion_why: whimsy + surprise -- a red-team game against an unbeatable AI bouncer is inherently shareable, and it doubles as a gut-check for anyone running an autonomous agent.

title: Borrowed-Authority Guard for Auto-Bet Agents
pitch: A tiny JS permission-compiler/rules-engine demo applying the paper's 'typed authority + evidence, not claims' idea to an autonomous betting bot: the agent can only place a bet if it holds verifiable evidence (matching odds snapshot hash, current bankroll state, an explicit signed limit) rather than trusting an injected 'user said go all-in' instruction. Includes a live attack-injection console showing which prompt-injection tricks get blocked.
discussion_why: decision-theory fit -- anyone running or considering an autonomous betting/trading bot has a real, current fear about it getting socially engineered into an unauthorized bet, and this makes that fear concrete and arguable.

title: Your AI Agent Can Be Social-Engineered Into Betting Your Life Savings
pitch: Explainer taking the paper's 'Borrowed Authority' attack pattern -- an agent trusting another agent's claimed permission instead of verifiable evidence -- and walking through how the same failure mode could hit an autonomous betting or trading bot, with the paper's 60/60-blocked defense as the fix pattern.
discussion_why: surprise + high relevance -- 'AI agent security research' reframed as 'your auto-bet bot is one prompt injection from yolo-ing your bankroll' is a direct hit for a betting/AI-curious audience.
